tool_input.command:
mkdir -p quizzes keys review-records && python3 -I - <<'EOF'
import json
q=json.load(open('drafts/0002-quiz.json')); k=json.load(open('drafts/0002-key.json'))
I={i['id']:i for i in q['items']}; K={i['id']:i for i in k['items']}
def opts(*t): return [{"id":c,"text":x} for c,x in zip("abcd",t)]
I['q1']['stem']="An expense tool receives a receipt photo. Design X: the code extracts the text, then asks a model for a spending category, then writes the entry to the ledger. Design Y: a model is given read_receipt, lookup_policy, flag_for_review and write_ledger tools and works out its own sequence. For one blurry receipt, the model in design X replies \"category unclear, skip the ledger\". What happens next in design X?"
I['q1']['options']=opts("The reply ends the run, since the model is the one that judged the receipt","The program carries on to its next written step, treating the reply as data","The model picks between writing the entry and stopping, using its tool list","The program pauses and asks the model which step should come after this one")
K['q1'].update(answer="b",rationale="In design X the developer's code owns the sequence; the model's reply is an output the program handles, not a decision about what runs next. Options a, c and d give the model control of the next step, which is what happens in design Y.")
I['q2']['stem']="A clinic's nightly job takes each new lab result, looks up the normal range, and sends the patient a templated message; a model only fills in the plain-language wording. Last night 12 messages went out with the wrong range. Why is the cause easier to reproduce and isolate when the job runs the same steps every night than when a model chooses its own tools?"
I['q2']['options']=opts("The model's wording varies between runs, so last night's messages cannot be compared","The wording step is the only part that uses a model, so the fault must be there","The job calls the model fewer times, so there is less output to read through","The same lookup runs every night, so last night's input can be rerun and compared")
K['q2'].update(answer="d",rationale="With fixed steps the range lookup runs the same way each time, so you can rerun it on last night's input and check it alone. Wording variation (a) exists in both designs, a model step is not automatically the culprit (b), and call count (c) is not what makes the fault reproducible.")
I['q3']['stem']="A data team's nightly report failed. Over the last month, three failures each needed different checks: a stale upstream table, an expired permission, and a schedule clash nobody had anticipated. The team wants an assistant that finds the cause of the next failure, including kinds it has not seen. Which design fits?"
I['q3']['options']=opts("The model chooses each check after seeing what the previous one returned, and stops once it has a cause","A fixed list of all known checks run in order, with the model summarising the results at the end","A fixed decision tree for the known causes, with the model only writing the final summary","One model call that reads the whole error log and names the cause without running any checks")
K['q3']['rationale']="Causes the team has never seen need checks nobody wrote down, so the model has to choose the next step from what it finds. A fixed list (b) or tree (c) only covers the known causes, and a single call with no checks (d) cannot gather missing information."
I['q4']['stem']="Your team compares two designs for a question-answering feature. The fixed workflow always runs 6 model calls per request. The agent version, on a typical request, asks for 2 tools one after another and then writes its answer; each model call ends with one tool request or the final answer. Assume every model call costs $0.01 and there are 300 requests a day. How many dollars per day does the agent version save on typical requests?"
K['q4'].update(answer=9,tolerance=0,rationale="The agent makes 2 tool-request calls plus 1 final-answer call = 3 calls: 3 x $0.01 x 300 = $9 per day. The workflow costs 6 x $0.01 x 300 = $18, so the agent saves $9. A fixed workflow is not always cheaper; it is cheaper when it needs fewer calls than the agent would. An answer of 18 or 9 for the wrong reason shows the call counts were not compared.")
I['q5']['stem']="Your makerspace assistant needs two features: (1) book a machine for a student who has given the machine, day and hour; (2) answer \"why did my 3D print fail?\" by working through the manuals, the maintenance log and the booking history. Which feature would you build as a fixed workflow and which as an agent?"
K['q5'].update(answer="Booking is a fixed workflow; the print diagnosis is an agent.",accepted=["1 workflow, 2 agent","feature 1 workflow, feature 2 agent","booking workflow, diagnosis agent","booking is a workflow and the diagnosis is an agent"],rationale="Booking has known steps in the same order every time (check the calendar, book, confirm), so code can own them; the diagnosis needs checks that depend on what each source shows, so the model must choose. Reversed is wrong. A correct assignment with a wrong reason is partial.")
I['q6']['stem']="An invoice assistant is a model with extract_fields, match_purchase_order and post_to_ledger tools, averaging 9 model calls per invoice. About 1 in 50 invoices is posted before it is matched. The team adds \"ALWAYS match before posting\" to the prompt and the rate drops to 1 in 200. Which next step best guarantees the order and keeps cost down?"
I['q6']['options']=opts("Make post_to_ledger refuse any invoice that has not been matched, and keep the loop","Add worked examples to the prompt until skipped matches drop to zero","Write the three steps as fixed code and use the model only to read fields","Switch to a larger model that follows long instructions more reliably")
K['q6'].update(answer="c",rationale="Every invoice goes through the same steps, so code should own the order: it guarantees it and removes the calls the model spent deciding what to do. A refusal check (a) blocks the bad post but keeps the 9-call loop and the retries; examples (b) and a larger model (d) lower the error rate without ever guaranteeing zero.")
json.dump(q,open('quizzes/0002.json','w'),indent=2); json.dump(k,open('keys/0002.json','w'),indent=2)
EOF
cat > review-records/0002-quiz.md <<'EOF'
# Review of quiz 0002 (objective O4)

Verdict: REVISE (4 serious, 6 minor findings).

Serious, all fixed:
- q2: absolute wording ("never", "would not help") in distractors; rewrote them as partly true claims and made the key differentiator "rerun last night's input and compare".
- q3: stem gave away the answer ("nobody can list the checks"); replaced with three concrete past failures, reworded options, made the decision-tree option a realistic hybrid.
- q6: stem stated the deciding fact ("same three steps"); removed it, stated the goal (guarantee order, keep cost down), made a refusal check a partly right distractor.
- q1: stem told the answer; added a twist (model replies "skip the ledger") so the learner must reason about who acts on the reply.

Minor:
- q5 key answer too long for exact-match solvers: shortened, added accepted variants. Recast on the makerspace assistant with a clearly open-ended diagnosis.
- q4 repeated quiz 0001's counting trick: changed to a case where the fixed workflow costs more.
- Overlap among q3/q5/q6 and flat difficulty: partly addressed (q1 now a reasoning item, q6 a find-the-flaw item); not restructured further, no second review.
- distractors: not added; the workspace has no misconception ids for these ideas and I did not invent any.
EOF

I also applied the cheap minor fixes and didn't ask for a second review. The one thing I left alone is that three items still lean on whether the steps are known in advance.
